title: The Talmud Torah, Synagogues, and Sokółka’s Religious Life
summary: The book’s many references to prayer houses and religious study show that these institutions were central to everyday communal life.
editorialContent:

## A spiritual quarter at the heart of town

In the memorial book, Sokółka’s religious life appears not as a single institution but as a close-knit landscape of classrooms, synagogues, study houses and Hasidic prayer rooms. The [Sokółka Jewish community](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_7ff6fd2ae75c09a88e55a665) gathered much of this life in the [Shulhof](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_a9e65e3090adf3adb7c9c8dd), the “synagogue courtyard” or square at the town’s spiritual center. A childhood recollection places the Great Synagogue, old and new batei midrash, Talmud Torah and Tarbut school together there: children learned, played and exercised within earshot of prayer and study. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/Sok209.html?utm_source=openai))

The wider record helps establish how old and substantial this communal presence was. Virtual Shtetl dates the first Jewish settlement in Sokółka to the second half of the seventeenth century and records Jewish privileges confirmed in 1698. It describes a Jewish quarter in the town’s southwestern part, with the main synagogue, old and new prayer houses, and the rabbi’s house. Its account dates the Main Synagogue to around 1900. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book’s view is more intimate than a town plan. It remembers religious institutions as neighbors and as part of children’s daily routes. The [Talmud Torah](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_b88cf9eb46add9184645a822) stood in the Shulhof; so did the [Great Synagogue](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_011708be9c3ac24db3082bd3), while the [Sokółka synagogue](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_54393c43e6ea8a46ae33e87f) appears in accounts of meetings, public speech and communal life. These references do not always identify which building is meant, so they should not be collapsed into a single synagogue.

## The Talmud Torah: learning across the community

The Talmud Torah gave religious education an organized, communal home. One memoir says that before the First World War, children from different economic circumstances attended: families who could afford it paid, while poorer children learned without charge. It recalls a local benefactor preparing new clothes for poor pupils before Passover. The same account remembers a voluntary treasurer, Herschel Ashkenowitz, and teachers including Daniel, Haim Yehuda Eksztein and “Shai” Adelsk. Another recollection names Yudel, the teacher from Odelsk, who devoted himself to explaining Torah and its interpretations. These are the book’s memories, rather than a complete register of pupils or staff. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691&utm_source=openai))

The records also associate the school with Rabbi Yitzhak Halevi and describe a preparatory yeshiva program. Other named teachers and workers include Samson Katzenellenbogen, Shmuel Cohen and Hershel Ashkenowitz, as well as Yudel from Madlask. The available evidence does not make clear whether all these people served at the same time, or how the preparatory program related to the Talmud Torah’s ordinary classes. It is safest to see them as strands in a longer institutional history, not as one fixed staff list.

The Talmud Torah existed alongside other kinds of education. A returning visitor to Sokółka lists it among the town’s traditional schools, alongside the heder associated with the Koznitzer teacher and schools run by Kaplan, Kunsht and Hillel Levin. The memorial book also distinguishes the traditional heder and Talmud Torah from the newer Tarbut school. One childhood account remembers the [Shulchan Aruch Beit Midrash](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_218e07fa598cdd6aa98d11d5), where the narrator studied Gemara and Midrash and where his father taught. Religious learning therefore ran through several settings, from children’s instruction to studyhouse debate. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/Sok165.html?utm_source=openai))

## One synagogue, several ways of gathering

The [Great Synagogue](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_011708be9c3ac24db3082bd3) was the most imposing worship space in the memorial book’s description. Its witness recalls a decorated Ark, a central bimah, colored-glass windows and a choir accompanying the cantor, especially on the High Holy Days. Yet the building was not equally comfortable in every season: another record says that, without heaters, prayer there was mainly held in summer. The book preserves both the grandeur of the building and the practical limits of worship in it.

Smaller batei midrash and shtiblekh gave religious life a more neighborhood-based and affiliated character. The [Kotsk Shtibl](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_433143e34162022bd329c70d) was in the Shulhof, and the [Karliner Shtibl](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_e06e46ed63d2d665ed91c461) offered a Karlin Hasidic place of prayer. The memoir’s scenes of singing and dancing on Simchat Torah, including movement between the main synagogue and the Karlin prayer house, suggest that worship could be both communal and particular: people shared festivals while maintaining distinct congregational centers. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok209.html?utm_source=openai))

Another memory recalls Rabbi Yisroel, known as “Der Novobranetz,” guiding young people at Tiferet Bachurim, a prayer room associated with the Great Synagogue. At Havdalah he would chant over a cup of wine, with the young people humming along; on Simchat Torah, the room became a place of exuberant celebration. Such testimony shows that the prayer houses were not merely smaller versions of the central synagogue. They could offer closer forms of instruction, fellowship and leadership for particular groups.

## Tradition within a changing town

Sokółka’s religious institutions stood beside changing cultural and political currents. The memorial book remembers the Tarbut school and Zionist activity as part of the same crowded neighborhood as the Talmud Torah and synagogues. It also records a tension in identity: children educated in the modern Hebrew school could be nicknamed “Tarbutniks” by Orthodox Jews and Talmud Torah pupils. The square was shared, but education shaped different social worlds. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691&utm_source=openai))

The broader record confirms that Sokółka was a significant Jewish center, though it cannot independently verify every classroom or prayer-room detail recalled by survivors. Virtual Shtetl reports 2,824 Jewish residents in 1897 and notes the community’s presence among the town’s artisans in 1936. The scale helps explain why the town sustained more than one educational and worship institution. For comparison, the memorial book describes the wider Sokółka region as having numerous synagogues and prayer halls, but that regional figure should not be mistaken for a count within Sokółka itself. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community?utm_source=openai))

The destruction of this religious landscape belongs to the story, too. A Yad Vashem encyclopedia entry exists for the Sokółka ghetto, while the town history on Wikipedia reports that the main synagogue was destroyed and the Jewish community was not restored. The memorial book’s own postwar recollections describe the former Great Synagogue as inaccessible and repurposed as a storehouse. These are distinct sources and distinct kinds of evidence: the memorial book preserves remembered places and loss; the outside accounts situate that loss within the Nazi occupation and the destruction of Sokółka’s Jews. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=691&utm_source=openai))

The [old synagogue](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_f4ef1a2227c04f7ec192c070), the New Synagogue and other prayer houses survive in the book as names attached to meetings, weddings and daily passage through town. Their precise locations and institutional histories remain threads for further research, as do the careers of several teachers and the relationship between the Talmud Torah and its preparatory yeshiva program. What the testimony makes clear is the pattern: study, worship and communal life were physically close, yet institutionally varied. Sokółka’s spiritual landscape was made by that combination.
